theme: War with Midian; Reuben and Gad settle east of the Jordan
readingInstruction: Read Numbers 31:1-32:42. These chapters describe the war against Midian and the request of two and a half tribes to settle east of the Jordan. The first is difficult material. Read it with care and with the context of the whole book in mind.
settingTheScene: God had told Moses that after the matter of Peor, he would take vengeance on the Midianites, and then he would be gathered to his people. Chapter 31 describes the campaign. Chapter 32 then turns to the tribes of Reuben and Gad, and half of Manasseh, who have large herds and see that the land east of the Jordan is good for livestock. They ask to settle there. Moses is alarmed, because it sounds like the sin of the spies all over again.
observation: God tells Moses, “Avenge the people of Israel on the Midianites. Afterward you shall be gathered to your people” (31:2).
Twelve thousand men, a thousand from each tribe, go out with Phinehas and the holy vessels (31:3-6).
They kill every male, including the five kings and Balaam son of Beor (31:7-8).
Moses is angry that the women who caused Israel to sin at Peor were spared (31:14-16).
The soldiers and anything that touched death must be purified (31:19-24).
The plunder is divided between the soldiers and the congregation, with a tribute to the LORD and to the Levites (31:25-47).
The tribes of Reuben and Gad ask to settle east of the Jordan (32:1-5).

Moses says, “Shall your brothers go to the war while you sit here?” and then agrees on the condition that they fight with the others until the land is taken (32:6-33). He warns, “Be sure your sin will find you out” (32:23).
interpretation:
The war with Midian is one of the more troubling stories in Scripture, and it deserves to be read honestly. It is presented as a judgment on a people who had deliberately tried to destroy Israel’s faith, and it is carried out as a holy war under God’s explicit command, under the leadership of the priest, and with the sacred vessels. It was not a general permission for violence. It was a specific judgment, in a specific time, on a specific people who had led Israel into idolatry.

Notice the attention to purity. The soldiers must be cleansed after the battle, and the plunder is purified. The text is clear that war is a defiling thing, even when commanded. The gold given to the LORD, 16,750 shekels, is accompanied by the confession that none of the men has been lost. These are the marks of a people who understand that they are not simply conquerors but servants.

The story of the eastern tribes is an important lesson about community responsibility. Reuben and Gad do not want to cross over. Moses’ first response is sharp, because he sees in it the same fear that destroyed their fathers. But the tribes explain that they will go before their brothers, armed, until the whole land is settled. Moses accepts, and he warns them that their word is binding before the LORD.

The sentence, “Be sure your sin will find you out,” is a proverb of its own. It is about the certainty that hidden or neglected obligations eventually come to light. Obligation to the community, kept or broken, is a matter of faithfulness to God.

The shape of the chapters is a warning against comfort. The tribes had found a good place and were tempted to stop short of the promise. We, too, can settle for good things this side of the Jordan. The call is to join our brothers in the greater work until it is done.
connection: Hebrews 4:11 says, “Let us therefore strive to enter that rest.” Paul tells believers to carry each other’s burdens (Galatians 6:2) and compares the church to a body (1 Corinthians 12). The warning to the eastern tribes echoes Jesus’ words about those who put their hand to the plow and look back (Luke 9:62). The war of Midian points to the ultimate battle against evil, which Christ has won (Colossians 2:15).
application:
Ask whether you have settled for something good that is short of God’s best for you.

Think about your obligations to your community. Are you carrying your share?

Consider the seriousness of sin. “Be sure your sin will find you out.” Confess anything hidden.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to keep you from settling short of his best.
Pray for those you walk beside, that you would be faithful to them.
Thank Christ for winning the final victory over evil.
